newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suez posts H1 profit, still dogged by property.
newsitem.headline: Suez posts H1 profit, still dogged by property.

text.p: French holding company Cie de Suez returned to profit in the first half of 1996 but continued to suffer from its disastrous real estate investments.
The company reported on Wednesday a net profit of 772 million francs ($148 million) for the first six months of 1996 after reporting a 1995 first half loss of 3.98 billion francs.

The result included a charge of 795 million francs against its real estate holdings, a considerable improvement from a year ago when the company was forced to take a 4.08 billion franc real estate charge.
All told, Suez has taken about 12.5 billion francs in charges since 1994 on its real estate investments.
On Wednesday, despite the healthy first-half profit, company chairman Gerard Mestrallet appeared to back away from earlier assertions that Suez would report a full-year profit for 1996.
Mestrallet answered merely "I hope so," when pressed on whether the company would be profitable this year.
He said Suez would show a pre-tax, pre-exceptional-item profit for the year.

"In conformity with a policy I adopted at (Suez unit) Societe Generale de Belgique, I will speak only of the pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit, which will in 1996 show growth compared to the previous year," he told a results news conference.
In 1995, the company's pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit was 1.62 billion francs.
In June, Mestrallet told the annual shareholders' meeting that "Suez will return to profit in 1996".

Suez is likely to continue to face hefty charges for property. It still has about 12.4 billion francs in real estate exposure, most of it grouped into a unit, Credisuez, which newspapers say Suez is trying to sell.
Mestrallet refused to comment on Credisuez, but said Suez was open to opportunities to shed real estate assets in line with the company's stated objective of leaving the real estate business by 2000.
Mestrallet said he remained committed to refocussing Suez's holdings on two core businesses: public utilities and infrastructure, and retail financial services.
"Our strategy is simple, it consists of refocusing on two core businesses," Mestrallet said.
The company said on Wednesday it was cancelling all of the current treasury shares in the company and redeeming in advance all of the convertible bonds issued in 1993.
The combined effect of these actions will be to eliminate about seven percent of the potential dilution to the company's present equity.
Mestrallet said the moves were "quite new for a large French company", and said they were aimed at increasing shareholder value.
"We want to deliver a message that our interest is to create value for our shareholders," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. ($ = 5.208 French Francs)
